question: What is Ceph, in plain terms, and what problem is it solving?
answer_html:
Ceph is an open-source, distributed storage system. Instead of storing your data on one big disk array or a single storage appliance, Ceph spreads it across a cluster of ordinary servers and disks, and makes that whole cluster look like one giant, highly available storage system to whoever is using it.

The problem it solves is the classic one with traditional storage: a single storage array is a single point of failure, it doesn't scale past the hardware you bought, and it's expensive to keep buying bigger boxes. Ceph instead says: take a bunch of commodity servers with disks, and let software handle replication, failure recovery, and scaling. You add more servers, the cluster grows. A disk or a whole server dies, the cluster heals itself and keeps serving data.

A useful analogy: think of Ceph like a self-organizing team of warehouse workers. Instead of one giant filing cabinet (a traditional SAN/NAS) that becomes a bottleneck and a liability if it breaks, you have many smaller cabinets spread across the warehouse, several copies of every document stored in different cabinets, and a smart dispatcher that knows exactly which cabinet has what — and reorganizes automatically if a cabinet is lost.

Critically, Ceph is unified storage: the same underlying cluster can present itself as block storage, file storage, or object storage at the same time, which is unusual — most systems specialize in one.

question: What is RADOS, and how does it relate to everything else in Ceph?
answer_html:
RADOS (Reliable Autonomic Distributed Object Store) is the foundation everything else in Ceph is built on. Every single byte that Ceph stores, no matter whether you're using it as block storage, file storage, or object storage, ultimately ends up stored as an object inside RADOS.

Think of RADOS as the engine room. It's the layer responsible for taking data, splitting it into objects, deciding where those objects physically live across the cluster, replicating or erasure-coding them for durability, and detecting and repairing failures automatically — all without a human having to intervene. "Autonomic" is the key word: RADOS is designed to self-manage.

On top of RADOS sit the interfaces users actually touch: RBD (block storage, e.g. virtual disks for VMs), CephFS (a POSIX-compliant shared filesystem), and RGW (an S3/Swift-compatible object storage gateway). All three are essentially client libraries or services that talk to RADOS and present its objects in a different shape.

This is why Ceph is called unified storage: RADOS doesn't care whether the objects it stores represent chunks of a virtual disk, a file, or an S3 bucket object — that distinction only exists one layer up.

question: Can you walk me through the main daemons that make up a Ceph cluster — OSD, MON, MGR, MDS?
answer_html:
A Ceph cluster is made of a handful of daemon types, each with a distinct job:

  • OSD (Object Storage Daemon): one OSD typically runs per physical disk (or per storage device). This is where the actual data lives. OSDs store objects, replicate them to other OSDs, and talk to each other directly to handle recovery and rebalancing. A cluster usually has many OSDs — dozens, hundreds, or thousands.
  • MON (Monitor): MONs keep the master copy of the cluster map — the source of truth for which OSDs exist, which are up, how data should be distributed (the CRUSH map), and the overall cluster state. MONs run in a small odd-numbered quorum (typically 3 or 5) using a Paxos-based consensus protocol, so the cluster keeps a consistent view of itself even if a MON goes down.
  • MGR (Manager): the MGR handles monitoring, metrics, and management functions — things like the dashboard, integration with external monitoring systems, and various built-in modules. It runs alongside the MONs and offloads work that doesn't need to be part of the strict consensus system.
  • MDS (Metadata Server): only needed if you use CephFS. The MDS manages filesystem metadata — directory structure, file names, permissions — so that file data itself can still be stored as plain objects in RADOS while the filesystem semantics are handled separately.

A simple way to remember it: OSDs hold the data, MONs hold the map of the cluster, MGRs watch and report on it, and MDS translates "this is a file called /foo/bar.txt" into RADOS objects when you're using CephFS.

question: What are CRUSH maps and placement groups (PGs), and why does Ceph need them?
answer_html:
When you store an object in Ceph, something has to decide exactly which disks, on which servers, that object's copies live on. Doing this lookup individually for every single object, and storing that mapping centrally, would not scale and would create a bottleneck and single point of failure. Ceph solves this with two related ideas: placement groups and the CRUSH algorithm.

A placement group (PG) is a logical bucket that a large number of objects get hashed into. Instead of tracking the location of millions of individual objects, Ceph only has to track the location of a much smaller, manageable number of PGs (typically each pool has somewhere from dozens to a few hundred PGs). Every object's name is hashed deterministically to a PG, so any client can compute which PG an object belongs to without asking a central server.

CRUSH (Controlled Replication Under Scalable Hashing) is the algorithm that then maps each PG to a specific set of OSDs. CRUSH uses a map of your physical infrastructure — which disks are in which servers, which servers are in which racks, which racks are in which data centers — called the CRUSH map, plus placement rules, to decide where replicas should go. Because it's a deterministic algorithm rather than a stored table, every client and every OSD can independently compute the same answer instantly, with no central lookup service and no bottleneck.

The analogy: PGs are like sorting mail into a fixed number of bins by zip code prefix instead of tracking every single letter, and CRUSH is the routing rule that decides which delivery trucks (OSDs) each bin gets assigned to, while making sure related bins don't all end up on the same truck (so one truck breaking down doesn't lose everything).

question: What happens inside a Ceph cluster when you write an object?
answer_html:
Say a client wants to write an object. First, the client computes which PG the object belongs to by hashing the object's name — no central server is involved in this step. Then it consults the current cluster map (obtained from the MONs) and runs the CRUSH algorithm to figure out which OSDs are responsible for that PG right now.

Each PG has one OSD acting as the primary for that PG, with the rest acting as replicas (in a replicated pool) or additional chunks (in an erasure-coded pool). The client sends the write directly to the primary OSD. The primary then forwards the write to the other OSDs responsible for that PG's replicas, and only acknowledges the write back to the client once enough replicas have confirmed it was durably written — this is what makes Ceph strongly consistent rather than eventually consistent.

Note that clients talk to OSDs directly, not through the MONs — the MONs only supply the map so everyone can compute placement independently. This direct-communication design is a big part of why Ceph scales well: there's no central gateway that all I/O has to funnel through.

question: What's the difference between replication and erasure coding for durability, and when would you choose one over the other?
answer_html:
Ceph pools (the logical containers data is stored in) need a durability strategy, and you generally pick one of two:

  • Replication: Ceph keeps multiple full copies of every object (commonly 3 copies, spread across different failure domains). It's simple, fast to read and write, and recovery just means copying a full copy from a surviving replica. The cost is storage overhead — 3x replication means you need 3 times the raw capacity of your usable data.
  • Erasure coding (EC): instead of full copies, data is split into fragments plus parity fragments (e.g., a "4+2" scheme stores 4 data chunks and 2 parity chunks across 6 locations, and can tolerate losing any 2 without data loss). This is much more storage-efficient than replication — you get strong durability at a fraction of the overhead. The trade-off is more CPU/network cost to reconstruct data during reads after a failure, and generally somewhat higher latency, which makes it less ideal for latency-sensitive, small, random-I/O workloads.

In practice, replication is favored for performance-sensitive workloads like RBD volumes backing databases or VMs, where low latency matters. Erasure coding is favored for large, less latency-sensitive, capacity-heavy workloads — the classic example being RGW object storage holding backups, media, or archives, where you want maximum usable capacity per dollar and read/write patterns are more sequential or bulk-oriented.

question: How does Ceph provide block storage (RBD), and what's it typically used for?
answer_html:
RBD (RADOS Block Device) presents a virtual block device — essentially a virtual hard disk — that's backed by objects striped across RADOS. When something writes to an RBD volume, Ceph internally chops that virtual disk into fixed-size objects (commonly a few megabytes each) and distributes those objects across many OSDs, just like any other RADOS object.

From the consumer's point of view — a VM hypervisor, a Kubernetes node via a CSI driver, or a physical machine with the RBD kernel module — an RBD volume just looks like an ordinary block device, e.g. /dev/rbd0, that you can partition and format with any filesystem. The consumer has no idea (and doesn't need to know) that underneath, that "disk" is actually scattered redundantly across dozens of physical drives on different servers.

This is the go-to Ceph storage type for things that need a normal disk abstraction with good performance: virtual machine disks (this is exactly what OpenStack Cinder and Proxmox commonly use Ceph for), and persistent volumes for containers via Kubernetes. RBD also supports handy features like thin provisioning, snapshots, and cloning, which make spinning up new VM disks from a golden image very fast.

question: How is CephFS different from RBD, and what does the MDS actually do during a file operation?
answer_html:
Where RBD gives you a block device (a raw disk that one client at a time typically mounts), CephFS gives you a full POSIX-compliant shared filesystem that many clients can mount and access concurrently — much like NFS, but backed by Ceph's distributed architecture instead of a single NFS server.

The key architectural difference is the MDS. File data is still just chopped into objects and stored in RADOS via OSDs, exactly like everything else in Ceph. But file metadata — directory hierarchy, filenames, permissions, timestamps, who has which files open — is managed separately by the MDS. When a client wants to open a file, it first asks the MDS to resolve the path and get the metadata (and a capability describing what it's allowed to do with the file); once it has that, the client talks directly to the relevant OSDs to read or write the actual file data, without going through the MDS again for the data itself.

This separation is why CephFS can support many concurrent clients safely reading and writing shared files/directories with normal filesystem semantics (locking, permissions, etc.) — the MDS coordinates who can do what, similar in spirit to how a lock manager works, while the bulk data path stays direct and fast between clients and OSDs.

Typical use cases: shared home directories, shared datasets for analytics/ML jobs, content repositories — anywhere multiple machines need to see the same files at once, which isn't really RBD's job.

question: What happens operationally when an OSD (or a whole node) fails? Walk me through self-healing.
answer_html:
This self-healing behavior is one of Ceph's defining features. When an OSD stops responding, the other OSDs (which constantly heartbeat each other) notice and report it. Once enough OSDs agree it's unreachable, the MONs mark it down in the cluster map, and after a further timeout, out — meaning it's no longer considered a valid location for data.

Marking an OSD out changes what CRUSH computes for every PG that OSD was responsible for: CRUSH now maps those PGs to a different set of OSDs. The cluster then automatically starts recovery — copying the missing replicas (or reconstructing erasure-coded fragments) onto the newly assigned OSDs from the surviving copies, until every PG is back to its target replica/fragment count. This all happens without any human triggering it.

There's a related but distinct process called rebalancing: whenever the cluster's OSD membership changes — you add capacity, remove a node, or an OSD comes back — CRUSH recomputes placement and data gradually migrates so it stays evenly spread across the new set of OSDs. Both recovery and rebalancing are throttled by default so they don't overwhelm client I/O, though the tuning between "heal fast" and "don't hurt production performance" is a real operational decision.

The practical upshot for an interviewer's follow-up ("so what do you actually do when a disk dies?"): usually nothing urgent — the cluster is already healing itself. The operator's job is to replace the physical disk, let the new OSD join, and keep an eye on cluster health status (`ceph status` / `ceph health`) to confirm it returns to HEALTH_OK.

question: What is a failure domain in Ceph, and how would you design CRUSH placement rules to survive a rack or a whole data center going down?
answer_html:
A failure domain is the boundary within which a single failure can take out multiple copies of your data at once — a disk, a host, a rack's power/network, or an entire data center/availability zone. The core design principle in Ceph is: never let two replicas (or too many erasure-coded chunks) of the same PG land inside the same failure domain, otherwise a single failure could destroy multiple copies simultaneously and you'd lose the data despite "having replicas."

By default, many Ceph deployments set the failure domain at the host level — meaning CRUSH guarantees that no two replicas of an object end up on OSDs in the same physical server, so losing one whole server only costs you one replica, not two. For a more resilient design, you'd model your physical topology into the CRUSH map (hosts nested under racks, racks nested under rows or data centers) and set the failure domain to rack or data center instead, so CRUSH spreads replicas across racks or sites, not just hosts. With 3x replication and a rack-level failure domain, an entire rack (power, top-of-rack switch, several hosts) can go dark and the cluster stays available and consistent.

The trade-off to raise proactively in an interview: the failure domain you choose has to be matched by enough physically independent domains and enough replicas/EC chunks to make it meaningful — e.g. you can't get real rack-level fault tolerance out of 3x replication if you only have two racks. Stretching this further, Ceph also supports stretch/multi-site cluster designs for surviving an entire data center loss, but that introduces real latency and consistency trade-offs since synchronous replication across sites is bounded by the speed of light and your network link.

question: Your Ceph cluster shows HEALTH_WARN with a large number of PGs stuck in a 'degraded' or 'undersized' state after a node failure, and client I/O is slow. How would you investigate and think about the trade-offs of fixing it fast versus safely?
answer_html:
First, I'd confirm what's actually happening rather than guess: `ceph status` and `ceph health detail` to see the overall state and PG counts, then `ceph pg dump` / `ceph osd tree` to see which OSDs are down and which PGs are affected. "Degraded" means some PGs have fewer copies than they should (a replica is missing, recovery is likely already in progress); "undersized" specifically means CRUSH currently can't even find enough distinct OSDs/failure domains to place the required number of replicas for some PGs — which is more concerning, since it hints the failure domain design or spare capacity is too thin for the failure that just happened.

For the slow client I/O, the likely cause is that recovery/backfill traffic (OSDs copying data to restore replica counts) is competing with client I/O for the same disks and network links. Ceph throttles this by default, but the tuning knobs — things like the recovery and backfill concurrency/priority settings — let you trade recovery speed against client latency. If the cluster is under-replicated and at real risk (e.g. one more failure would mean actual data loss), I'd lean toward prioritizing recovery speed even at some client latency cost. If data is merely degraded but still safely above minimum replica counts, I'd throttle recovery down and protect client-facing performance instead, since the risk of data loss is lower.

I'd also check whether the failed node was a single point that legitimately shouldn't have caused "undersized" — e.g. if the failure domain is host-level but there aren't enough remaining hosts to satisfy placement rules for the affected pools, that's a capacity/design problem, not just a transient blip, and the actual fix is adding hosts or adjusting the pool's size/min_size, not just waiting.

Finally, I'd watch `min_size` specifically: if min_size for a pool is set equal to its full replica count, any single further failure during recovery would block writes entirely (Ceph refuses to serve writes below min_size to protect consistency), which is a common cause of "I/O froze" incidents during a cascading failure — so I'd sanity check that min_size is set to tolerate at least one more failure during the recovery window.

question: An interviewer asks: 'We already use cloud-native block and object storage (like EBS/S3 or Azure Disk/Blob). Why would anyone run Ceph themselves instead?' How would you answer that?
answer_html:
I'd frame it as a trade-off between control and operational burden, not a claim that Ceph is universally better. Cloud-native services like S3 or EBS are excellent when you're fully committed to one cloud, want zero operational overhead, and are comfortable with that provider's pricing and data-egress model. Ceph becomes attractive specifically when one or more of those assumptions break down.

  • Avoiding cloud lock-in / multi-cloud or hybrid needs: Ceph runs the same way on-prem, in any cloud, or across both, giving one consistent storage layer and API (including an S3-compatible interface via RGW) instead of re-architecting storage per environment.
  • Cost at scale: at large capacities, especially for object storage, self-run Ceph on commodity hardware can be meaningfully cheaper than metered cloud storage plus egress fees — this is exactly why many large-scale hosting providers and research institutions run it themselves.
  • Data sovereignty / regulatory constraints: some organizations (government, finance, healthcare, certain countries) are required to keep data on infrastructure they fully control, ruling out public cloud storage for some workloads regardless of cost.
  • Unified storage needs: needing block, file, and object storage from one system with one operational model, rather than stitching together separate cloud services with different consistency and access models.

The honest trade-off to acknowledge: you take on real operational responsibility — capacity planning, hardware failures, upgrades, and needing staff who actually understand CRUSH maps, PGs, and failure domains, exactly the kind of knowledge this conversation is testing. That operational cost is exactly why plenty of teams reasonably choose managed cloud storage instead, and why the right answer is genuinely "it depends on your scale, constraints, and in-house expertise," not "Ceph is always better."
